parts.text: Professor Terence Tao, from Unversity of California, Los Angeles, is one of the world’s leading mathematicians and a prominent

of AI’s use in mathematics. He recently coined the term “proof digestion” for the many ways that mathematicians continue to work with a proof after its correctness has been established.

They may reorganise the proof around more natural concepts,

a complicated argument, connect it to existing mathematics, or extract methods that can be applied elsewhere. Proof digestion itself can be highly fruitful and produce new mathematics.

Continuing work

Even after a proof has been digested, the

work is rarely done. Major mathematical results often become stepping stones towards new open problems. Important variants of the Navier-Stokes problem, for example, cannot be solved by the methods of the recent proof proposed by OpenAI. This is

of major breakthroughs: their importance often lies not only in answering a long-standing question, but also in introducing novel mathematical concepts and opening up new lines of research.

Often, one proof simply is not enough. Mathematicians

search for new proofs of results that have already been proven. Take, for example, the Pythagorean Theorem: a² +b² = c². This relates to the three lengths of a right-angled triangle.

This result was proved in antiquity, yet a book published in the 1920s

more than 300 proofs for the Pythagorean Theorem that have been established over the last two millennia. If the only purpose of a proof is to establish that a result is true, all but the earliest of these proofs would be

.

Instead, the opposite is the case: different proofs may reveal new insights into why the result is true, uncover new connections to concepts from other mathematical areas, or suggest new methods of generalisation. Thus, proofs are not only valued for

mathematical results, but also for the explanation and understanding they provide.

What exactly makes a proof explanatory or illuminating is difficult to pin down – and remains an ongoing topic in the

of mathematics. This makes explanation and understanding much less clear goals for AI than simply producing a correct proof.

The recent advancements in AI will likely transform mathematical practice profoundly. But mathematics is not simply the production of correct answers to
problems. Proofs still need to be understood, reorganised, connected to other results and used to generate new questions.
